notes.meaning: God's heavy judgment rests upon the land of Hadrach and the city of Damascus, a longtime enemy of His people. At the same time, the eyes of all humanity and of Israel are turned toward the Lord to see what He will do. God rules all nations as well as His own people, so every empire must answer to Him.

The neighboring city of Hamath to the north will share in this judgment, along with the wealthy coastal trading cities of Tyre and Sidon. These cities thought they were exceedingly clever and could save themselves by their own skill and trade. Yet human craftiness can never turn aside the righteous judgment of God.

Tyre built strong island walls and piled up silver and gold until riches seemed as common as dirt in the streets. In spite of this wealth, the Lord promised to strip away her defenses, cast her strength into the sea, and burn the city with fire. This prophecy came to pass when Alexander the Great used the rubble of the old city to build a causeway and conquer the island fortress.

The southern cities of Philistia tremble in terror as they watch the fall of mighty Tyre. Gaza writhes in agony, Ekron loses all hope of rescue, and Ashkelon is emptied of its people. When the world powers that people rely on fall, those who trust in them are left with nothing but fear.

Foreigners and mixed populations will settle in Ashdod, replacing the native inhabitants. God promises to bring a complete end to the stubborn pride and boasting of the Philistines. Human arrogance cannot withstand the humbling hand of the Lord.

God will put an end to their pagan feasts where they ate idol sacrifices and meat with blood. The surviving Philistines will turn to the true God and be welcomed into His household, just as the ancient Jebusites were folded into Jerusalem under King David. God's grace has the power to transform old enemies into fellow worshipers.

God promises to set up camp around His house to guard His people from invading armies marching through the land. While worldly conquerors sweep back and forth, God watches over His own with His personal care so they are not wiped out. His people are kept safe under His constant protection.

The people of Jerusalem are told to shout for joy because their promised King is coming to them. He is perfectly righteous, brings salvation—which means rescue from sin and danger—and comes in humble meekness, riding on a young donkey instead of a war horse. Jesus fulfilled this prophecy when He entered Jerusalem on Palm Sunday as the Prince of Peace.

The coming King will take away the chariots, war horses, and battle bows because His kingdom does not depend on worldly weapons. He will speak peace to all nations, bringing an end to hatred and war. His gentle reign will stretch from sea to sea and reach to the farthest corners of the earth.

differ.view: Verse 9 was fulfilled at Jesus' first coming, while verse 10 awaits a future fulfillment when Christ returns to establish a literal earthly millennium of peace.
Both verses describe Christ's spiritual kingdom, which began at His first coming and continues to spread peace to the nations through the gospel.

notes.meaning: God speaks to His people and promises to free their captives from waterless pits, an image of hopeless dungeons and bitter exile. He grants this release because of the blood of His covenant, which is a solemn, binding promise sealed by sacrifice. This rescue pointed ahead to how the blood of Christ frees sinners from the prison of guilt and death.

differ.view: The covenant blood points back to God's unconditional covenant of grace made with Abraham in Genesis 15.
The covenant blood refers to the covenant established at Mount Sinai, where Moses sprinkled sacrificial blood on the people.

notes.meaning: The Lord invites the exiles to run to their safe stronghold, calling them prisoners of hope because His promises give them a bright future. Even in their lowest distress, He declares that He will repay them double the blessing and comfort for all their past suffering. Christ is the true refuge where believers find shelter from every trial.

God pictures Judah as His battle bow and Ephraim as the arrow He fits onto the string. He raises up the sons of Zion to fight like a warrior's sword against the armies of Greece. This was fulfilled when Jewish Maccabean fighters resisted Greek oppressors, and it foreshadows God using His church to overcome the powers of the world.

The Lord Himself will appear above His people to lead and defend them, shooting His arrows of judgment like lightning. He will blow the trumpet to rally His forces and charge forward like a whirlwind from the south. The victory belongs entirely to the Lord, who fights for those who trust Him.

The Lord of Hosts shields His fighters so they can trample down the slingstones hurled against them. They shout with the joy and boldness of men cheered by wine, filled with the presence of God. Their triumph is as complete as the sacrificial bowls and altar corners drenched with blood.

On that day the Lord will rescue His people with the loving care of a shepherd tending his flock. Instead of being trampled down like common stones, they will sparkle across His land like jewels set in a royal crown. God views His redeemed people as His most precious and honored possession.

The chapter closes with wonder at how great God's goodness and beauty are toward His people. Plentiful grain and fresh wine will make the young men and women thrive with strength and joy. God delights to replace the starvation of exile with the rich blessings of His presence.
